met:443592.summary: Woven in red and cream on this fragile band are the first events of Christ's life, set within little architectural frames and read from right to left: the Annunciation, the bathing of the newborn Christ, the Nativity with the Child lying in a stone manger, and the Adoration of the Shepherds. Though only fragments survive, the clear outlines of figures and buildings remain legible. A band like this may once have adorned a tunic, carrying the Gospel story on everyday dress.
facts: The Met notes that the bathing of the Christ Child was a popular motif not recorded in the Gospel texts.
It is woven in warp-faced compound twill of wool, linen and silk, and was made in Syria though found in Egypt.
The band came to the Met in 1890 as a gift of George F. Baker.

walters:71.113.summary: Under a pierced canopy carried on twisted columns, Christ hangs on the cross with arms spread wide and head inclined, while the Virgin raises her hands toward him and St John, holding a Gospel book, gestures in grief. At the foot of the cross a small rounded form, perhaps the skull of Adam, marks Golgotha. The figures have rounder faces and softer drapery than most ivories of their time.
facts: The Walters notes that the canopy and the softer, rounder style set this plaque apart from its contemporaries, and associates it with the Nikephoros Group, named after Emperor Nikephoros II.
Holes at each corner were used to fasten the wings of the triptych of which it was the centre.
walters:71.113.notes: The possible skull at the foot of the cross is my reading of the photograph; the museum does not mention it.
